utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances. For the OTP, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian and Ann Sutherland assisted by Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately, we are not able to continue immediately with our witness. But I learned, and I am quite sure, that nothing else will happen that we can continue at 5.00, as scheduled, with the witness. Nevertheless, we have numerous questions to resolve today. But first of all, I want to invite the parties, are there any new observations to be made? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually perhaps, if we have extra time this afternoon, we could meet in Chambers briefly as a 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary, first of all, to discuss the pending motions. There are two, one of the OTP. The third notice for admission of transcript and statement pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Chamber is prepared, and it was said in the hearing of -- let me find out -- of Monday, 10th of June, that it should be decided today. May I hear the observations by the Defence as regards the six witnesses on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you. On behalf of the Defence, we have evaluated the statements and the transcripts provided by the Office of the Prosecution and have an objection to 65 ter number 36, dated July 16th, 2001, specifically described in the motion as a 92 bis statement. I can elaborate with respect to that particular witness, 65 ter number 36, but for the record, initially, I'd like to state that we do not have an objection to the documents as identified in the motion by the Prosecution under 65 ter number 20, which is the Omarska transcript of that individual witness, taken on October 3rd and 4th of the year 2000. Likewise, we do not have an objection to 65 ter number 32 described in the OTP motion as the Omarska transcript, dated June 7th, 2000. Moreover, we do not have an objection to Witness 65 ter number 42 and the description, as offered by the OTP in their motion, as a 92 bis statement dated January 11th, 1996. We also have no objection to the ICTY signed statement as described of Witness Number 16, date of statement: October 9th, 2000. And finally, Your Honour, we do not have an objection to Witness 65 ter Number 27 of a signed statement dated March 13th and 14th of the year 2000. With respect to Witness 65 ter Number 36, we do have an objection specifically because we believe that the witness's statements fall outside the provisions required to be submitted as a 92 bis witness. There are allegations or statements made in the statement which are conclusory, which go to the heart of the issues as they appear in the fourth amended revised indictment against Dr. Stakic. In light of that, we would ask the Court to either prevent this witness live or reject the motion as it relates to this witness or present the witness at the very least for purposes of cross-examination on behalf of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. May we go through the witness number by number. I have the impression your answer was detailed and, to a certain extent, sophisticated. But to be quite clear, as Witness Number 16, the Trial Chamber does not withdraw former observations that they regard it, especially in view to the detailed fourth amended indictment, that this witness should be heard either as a live witness or by the means of a videoconference. Is it the understanding of the Defence that, on the basis of the written statements available, made available by the OTP, it is not necessary to hear this witness, even not for the purposes of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As stated, Your Honour, with respect to Witness Number 65 ter Number 16, we do not have an objection to merely the submission of the ICTY's signed statement dated October 9th, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any additional comments from the OTP? To 65 ter Number 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Number 20 or Number 36?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, 16 is already resolved. Now we are with 65 ter Number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Number 20, we believe is a crime-based witness. I don't believe there's an objection from the Defence to Number 20. They were objecting to Number 36 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just wanted to go through witness by witness. Then the documents provided as regards Witness Number 20 are admitted under Rule 92 bis. What about 27? It's my understanding that there were no objections at all by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then also these statements are introduced under 92 bis. My understanding was there were no principal objections by the Defence, as regards Witness 32, but the Trial Chamber doubts whether it wouldn't be necessary to have some more information. First of all, on the role of the Territorial Defence, one could conclude from the statements before us that (redacted) (redacted) and he can give us some detailed descriptions on Omarska camp and that what happened to the parents there. So therefore, the Chamber is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I be heard on that, Your Honour. As to Number 32, this witness has testified. This witness testified -- I believe your microphone is on. This witness testified about what he experienced, which was that as a very young adult, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: (redacted). There's nothing to be gained by making him come back and repeat that testimony we feel, again. I spoke to this witness, Your Honour, personally, and his wife. They had great difficulty recovering from the trauma of testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We understand this point. Observations from your side, taking into account once again these observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I think, Your Honour, with respect to 65 ter witness number 32 we do not object that the transcript be introduced as evidence, so long as it's in its whole, both the direct and cross-examination questions, and other than that, we don't want to have the witness exposed to any unnecessary further trauma that he may sustain from either being questioned or recollecting on those events. So we have no objection to it

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The statements of 65 ter witness number 32, including the cross-examination is admitted under Rule 92 bis as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I request a redaction from the transcript of my argument because I gave some information that would identify the witness. And also I believe at 16.10.38, Your Honour indicated the position of the father of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm just signing this document. Now, coming now to Witness 65 ter Number 36, and there were some observations against the admission under 92 bis, and I want to recall that the Trial Chamber, already in the past, has indicated that this should be a witness, a witness to be heard, first of all as long as the killings in the -- the alleged killings in the Benkovac barracks form still part of the fourth amended indictment. And until now, we didn't hear any witness on this issue. It could be Witness Number 42, but we can't have both under 92 bis. So therefore, although here it's true what we stated as regards Witness Number 16, the Trial Chamber invites the OTP either to hear this witness under -- as a live witness or, and here I need some other observations by the Defence, would the Defence agree that this witness would be heard by the means of a videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As in the past, the Defence will cooperate in any way with the Trial Chamber's suggestions and with any suggestions that the OTP may have with processing the witnesses, whether live or through videolink. We would just like, as stated earlier, to have an opportunity to cross-examine this witness, by the means available and provided by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, therefore, in principle, we should like to hear this witness as a live witness. If not possible, by the means of a videolink. Let's finally turn to 65 ter Number 42. And given that Number 36 is available now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As stated earlier, Your Honour, we do not have an objection to the acceptance into evidence of Witness 65 ter number 42 and its 92 bis statement dated January 11, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you are aware of the fact that -- probably I'm wrong -- but this is the only witness testifying about Serb attack, the alleged Serb attack on the villages of Kevljani and Jakupovici?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the statement of 65 ter Witness Number 42 is admitted under Rule 92 bis. This concludes the discussion of the motion of the OTP. The other motion was the one by the Defence. And I have to ask the OTP whether or not the OTP is prepared to respond, or does the OTP regard it necessary to respond in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We would like to do whatever Your Honours prefer. We can respond orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, if you are prepared, then do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's rather a general motion, so it's difficult to respond in concrete terms without having a particular question in front of us. But speaking in general terms, our case against the accused, as Your Honours have seen, is based upon, not his presence at the scene of crimes, not -- we're not going to present evidence of a direct order to commit murders, but our evidence, we're trying to show in this case that in 1992, during the time that the accused was in a position of great responsibility and described as the "number one man" in Prijedor, events were taking place throughout the municipality on such a scale that it was -- it would be impossible for a person in that position to take no action, that if he was doing that, that by that, he was aiding and abetting and furthering the scheme. Our position is that each of the crimes discussed by the witnesses that come here and testify for, perhaps a day or two, they are talking about what they experienced, and really they are telling you about -- to use an American analogy, about individual trees, and our case is the forest. We need Your Honours to see the entire forest. But a witness can only come in and talk about a particular crime and individual trees that they saw. It's impossible for them to relate everything that they observed throughout 1992 or the period of this indictment. Sometimes we ask a witness, based upon their presence during that time period, about their general impressions and observations about what was taking place. I think that that can be a proper question in the proper context because witnesses are telling you at that time about the forest, about how it was obvious to anyone who was present at the scene that what was going on, for example, was not individual crimes unrelated, but crimes that were taking place in an organised and orchestrated fashion. It's not our intent to have these witnesses answer questions as an expert, but these are all people who experienced what happened in 1992. All of us are trying to recreate what it was like back there ten years ago, from a position far, far removed. And while we can get details about individual incidents that happened, I think it's also helpful to get the impression of someone who was present and lived through those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any comments in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. What I think the Court, respectfully, has heard from the Office of the Prosecution is an argument that witnesses should be allowed to testify on issues relating to matters of fact and observations. Our motion, respectfully, goes well beyond that. Our motion goes to opinion testimony which was previously undisclosed in violation of the rules that we must adhere to here before the International Crimes Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. Those rules specifically state that when a witness, despite the fact that, in addition to having opinions, is also a fact witness, must be disclosed as an opinion witness. And we, the Defence, should not be surprised on the eve of trial, as it was with the current witness, Mr. Sejmenovic, to get a written statement dated July 11th, 2002, and his testimony commencing on June 12th, 2002. If we read those statements from that witness in particular, and from others that are coming down the pipe as we see them, it is a direct violation of that rule. Mr. Sejmenovic can testify, and we invite him to testify about the events that he, himself personally saw, experienced, and recollects. However, if we take the events of his three prior sworn testimonies that he provided to the Tribunal on three separate occasions, and his one prior written statement given last year in 2001, it is impossible, and it is not practical, to see that the witness that is provided here starts in its June 11th, 2002 statement by saying: "I have been given numerous documents to review, immediately prior to my testimony." If the OTP can show me where in its prior statement or in the three prior times that this witness has testified before this Tribunal, where he was once mentioned that he has in preparation reviewed any such documents or is offering any opinions close to those that he highlights on page 2 of his June 11, 2002, statement. In order to put it in better perspective and in context, this witness was called as a witness in July of 1998 before a trial with the defendant named Milan Kovacevic. Similarly, the indictment in this case is against a member purportedly of the Crisis Staff. At that time, the opinions were not solicited from this witness because he was a fact witness. Now, because of some change, either in strategy or positioning, they have decided to expand this witness's prior testimony and knowledge, having shared with him documents which I hope I will be given latitude to examine him on, which documents, et cetera, for purposes of forming conclusory opinions that not only other experts will be formulating for this Chamber, but also respectfully that this Chamber will be formulating on its own based on the evidence and the documents. So our motion is not just a general motion; it's specifically addressed to the problem that we see, not only with this witness Mr. Sejmenovic, but with other witnesses when the rules are quite clear, in our opinion crystal clear, as to what the notice provisions, and obligations and duties by the OTP for giving proper notice to the accused in order to ensure that he has a fair trial. We respectfully think that those rules have been violated by virtue of the witness statement that was provided to us on the eve of Mr. Sejmenovic's testimony. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just, for clarification, ask, because reading very carefully your motion, I didn't really understand, is this motion related to several witnesses, or to the testimony of Mr. Sejmenovic only?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When the motion, Your Honour, was quite honestly initially drafted, it was to address what we believe is a general practice that we didn't want to get ambushed during the testimony. Interestingly enough, the timing of the motion could not have been better, in my opinion, and it relates specifically to this witness now, because that's the witness before us. We hope that the problem doesn't arise again. We think that particularly, it's a most timely as it relates to Mr. Sejmenovic. Because if we look through his statement on pages 2, and specifically pages 3, there are clear, conclusory opinions based on his review of these numerous documents." So if necessary, I'll revise our motion so that it would be specific for Mr. Sejmenovic, but at the time when it was initially drafted, it was -- since we saw from prior witnesses in our opinion that some of their testimony seemed to be either borderline opinion testimony or even beyond that borderline level which we felt comfortable. And therefore, we decided to present that motion as a general motion, but orally we're specifically insisting, respectfully, that the motion apply to this witness Mr. Sejmenovic in light of his June 11th, 2002 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you're aware that the motion as it reads now may be -- we haven't discussed it yet as a Bench -- may be not admissible because being not concrete enough and leaving it open to which witnesses it shall be related. And therefore, I think it would be preferable to have a more concrete motion on Mr. Sejmenovic only, if you so want. Or, to be more concrete. Otherwise probably, the Bench would have to say we don't know what is the scope of application of your motion because you mention only the words -- I quote from the top of my head -- "previous witnesses" and leaving it open what is really the subject matter of the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We, we would orally, unless the Court would like it in writing to amend and revise our motion so that it specifically incorporates the arguments we presented to the Court today to be limited, so that there's no doubt about it, to at least this witness and when the time is ripe, we will obviously make a decision and most likely if the issue arises again would file another motion and be more specific with the witnesses in which we believe that go beyond what has previously been identified as their testimony. However, I'd like to only add one other point: It is difficult for the Defence to anticipate that anyone will violate the rules that are provided here. So we are not saying that the OTP has violated the rules with any future witnesses, but we think that it's a motion that necessarily would put all of us on guard with further having respect and understanding of those rules and allowing the defendant to have a fair trial by giving the proper notice. If proper notice was given of this witness's opinions, we wouldn't be arguing this point here now. With respect to future experts that they have, we have their opinions, and the bases for those opinions. So we're not raising an objection for those expert witnesses. I can, for the court, if it likes to elaborate on the prior witnesses that we believe were borderline but I'd rather reserve that right and bring it by way a of a written motion with the transcripts attached as exhibits, comparing that to the prior documents or testimony that were provided to us relating to the substance of their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe the best would be if you prepare a new motion based on the concrete witness before us at present, and then we can concentrate our response and our decision on this issue and, thereby, hopefully facilitate the cooperation in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just one observation: Part of the difficulties that we face is due to the rather unique nature of this institution. Many of the witnesses, particularly the witnesses from the Prijedor area, were first interviewed back in about 1995, 1996 where they were asked for all of their experiences during the war. Many of these statements have been used in cases involving particular camps or statements involving co-accused. It's always the case that when a witness comes to The Hague, there are going to be more specific questions that the lawyer that's going to present that witness has for the witness. We try to give the Defence as much notice as possible, but providing proofing notes that, in this case, Ms. Korner because she recognised that there were significant additions by Mr. Sejmenovic and the importance of him as a witness went the further step of getting a signed statement. But the reality is 65 ter only requires a summary of the facts the witness is going to testify to, and all of us are faced with the fact that we're always going to think of and Your Honours are going to think of additional questions that haven't been asked previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I believe we should leave it for today, and we expect a new motion substituting the motion before us and being more concrete and more to the point. And because of the fundamental question raised here, it will be then decided in writing. The third question is now, was it possible for the OTP to present, as it was stated the 10th of June, as regards all the documents related to Dr. Stakic in person, be it a clip, newspaper, be it an unsigned document, be it a signed document by whomsoever, was it possible to present this document in the "most original version"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we have so far is collected those documents that we believe have the signature of the accused on them that have been admitted into evidence. There's an additional list of documents that may be coming up later and documents that we believe the accused is responsible for, for example, if it says "Crisis Staff" without a signature. But we have in this binder the documents that were seized. These are the originals from the evidence unit, which we could present to the Defence counsel and the Court, of those documents with signatures that we believe are the accused, that have been admitted into evidence to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that during the next break, the Defence is discussing this issue together with the accused? Because it's also a fundamental right of the accused to have a look at these documents in person. I don't think it's appropriate to do this in our presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We agree. And we'll accomplish that, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, I don't want to continue on the fourth issue, which, of course, is a question of signatures, right now. As indicated beforehand in the remaining time until 5.00, it is for us to proceed with reading out a few documents. And I emphasise, with a view to the booth, "a few documents" only, from the lists 2 and 3. Please correct me if I am wrong, but I think the next would be 73 in the order we find in list 2. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I be excused so I can bring those documents so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, can we proceed. We are grateful to hear that it's possible that the document will be read out in B/C/S, and we have it then available in French and English as well. Document S73. I think we can start now. utterances.text: Do the parties agree that we can continue now on point 2 without reading out the single buildings? I can see no objections. Please continue with paragraph 2. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.text: We do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's one of the documents, we're talking about Number 73, I believe, that we do have --
