utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally before our break, the next document, that would be Document S78.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to go back, just for a moment on the last document, in the transcript it indicated the date at 16.65, June 1993. I believe it's 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It should read 1992. It's not contested. So may we then, please, hear Document S78. THE INTERPRETER OF THE REGISTRAR: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff. Number 02-111-202/92. Date: 16th of June, 1992. "At its meeting of the 16th of June, 1992, Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff, pursuant to Articles 3 and 7 of the decision on the organisation and work of Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff issued the following order, relating to the manner of requisitioning MTS, materiel and technical equipment, and supplies, and the control thereof: "Order: One, requisitioning of MTS and equipment for the needs of the army, police, and other structures shall be carried out strictly by order and at the request of municipal secretariat for people's defence. "Two: Prijedor garrison command and the public security station are hereby obliged to identify their requirements for MTS and supplies and to submit them as per establishment to the municipal secretariat for people's defence so that MTS and supplies, which have already been taken by the army and police, may be legalised in keeping with their actual requirements. "Three: Control over goods in storage and available MTS may be exercised only by authorised persons/inspectors of the economy and social affairs and the municipal revenue administration. "Four: Directors of all enterprises, organisations and associations are hereby obliged to inform the municipal Crisis Staff, without delay and in writing, of any continuing unauthorised exercise of control over, or requisitioning of, stored goods and MTS. "Five: This order shall enter into force on the day it is issued." Lower left corner: "Sent to: One, the above-mentioned. Two, files." Lower right corner: "President of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic." Signed and stamped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we have our break now, it was said that during the break, the Defence will have the possibility to discuss the documents provided by the OTP with the accused. But immediately after the break, we have to turn to the testimony of our present witness. And after the hearing of today, I should like to see the parties for a short meeting in my office, 5 minutes after the finalisation of this hearing. The trial stands adjourned until 5.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Sometimes even in these premises, surprises happen. And we can continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was in fact here at 5 to 5.00, but I am very grateful, Your Honour, for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Defence may be quite sure that just in case they can or they run into difficulties of the same nature, we will show the same patience no doubt. But please, start immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, at the end of Thursday's session, you had just dealt with effectively the attack on Kozarac and what happened to the people there. What, in fact, did you do after the attack? Where did you go? And I don't mean immediately afterwards because we dealt with that, but in the ensuing days until you went to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During several days afterwards, I joined the people who were escaping. As I've already explained, for several days and on several occasions, I moved between the Trnopolje area, through the village of Sivci to the village of Hrnici, that is, to a place which is about half a kilometre far from Kozarac. On the third day, I began to hide. And this hiding went on for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you what you witnessed during the time that you were hiding. Did you see a number of operations being carried out by Serbs in various villages?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw several such operations, the so-called cleansing of the villages. They were looking for and arresting the extremists, and then they were mopping up the villages which had been emptied of their inhabitants during the operations. Considering the position in which I was hiding, that was just on the borderline between three villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have again the map you were looking at last Thursday, please. I've forgotten what the number is. S146, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I wonder if I could have a copy myself. Perhaps we better have it on the ELMO. I think it's probably better on the ELMO. Close enough for the witness to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just indicate roughly the area, by pointing on to the map, where you were hidden those first couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will show you quite accurately. This area here, between the village of Hrnici, Mujkanovici, Jaskici, and Gornji Sivci. Here you can see the village of Sivci. So, close above is the village of Gornji Sivci. The area I'm pointing at now is the border line between these villages. Operations were carried out in each of these villages, but also the area which I was was covered by the operation, so that when the operation took place, the village of Hrnici, also this area was covered. Then the village of Mujkanovici and then the village of Gornji Sivci. Each time, I could watch the actions taken place as part of the operations that were being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. What I'm going to ask you about, those operations. You said earlier that they were looking for and arresting "the extremists." What do you mean by the "extremists?"

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the very first operations, after the burning of Kozarac, when the Serb army started to enter areas where the population was concentrated, at first, they came in with the explanation that they were only looking for extremists, that is, members of the SDA or people that had weapons in their possession. However, the next step clearly demonstrated that that wasn't true because they were arresting all men and taking them away somewhere. At first, we didn't know where, but later on we found out where. During each of the operations, they killed several people. Almost as a rule, in a group of 30 houses, there would, as a rule be two or three victims. People were killed in their houses, on the way to their houses, or just outside their houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The people who were killed, was that random killing or because they tried to run away or tried in some way to resist?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were random killings. For example, in the village of Sivci, two old men were killed and two women, as far as I can remember. In the village of Hrnici, three men and one woman were killed. In the village of Elezi, a number of men and women were killed, mostly old people. And so in these waves of extermination, of cleansing the villages, there was no selection. Those were random killings of civilians. And afterwards, there were threats to the effect that whoever was found in their homes would be killed. So it was for these reasons that people started moving towards Trnopolje, as the Serb army had told them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You talked about "they," the Serbs, who do you mean by that? Was this army or police, or a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant all of them. Very often, the units carrying out this so-called ethnic cleansing were composed of JNA soldiers, soldiers we could still recognise as JNA soldiers, soldiers from the Serbian Krajina in Croatia, many soldiers and half-civilians who only had a military shirt but wore plain trousers. These operations were carried out in a coordinated way by all of them. So it was difficult to say whether it was being done by the JNA, the police, or whoever. It was a mixture of all these different factors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you, yourself, witness these events that you've described, the killings and the rounding up and all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever an operation took place, someone would usually escape. So we got in touch with these people later on because we were hiding together, and then those people would tell us what they had seen. We only heard sounds of shooting as close as a hundred metres from our house and as far as two kilometres, but not more than that. Very close to the place where I was, a primary school teacher was killed, maybe three or four hundred metres further down from the house where I was. And at approximately the same distance in the village of Sivci, the old people that I have referred to were killed, and they were buried the same evening behind the houses in that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the events you described, you learned from people who came from these places. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both them and the people who had buried the bodies. As far as the killings themselves are concerned, I did not watch the killings personally, but I did watch the army escorting the captured civilians down the road to Trnopolje. I watched this from close by on one occasion; and on another occasion, I watched it from an abandoned house. On a third occasion, I watched this through a hedge behind which I was, and the hedge was very close to the road down which they were going. So these are the things that I could see myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The accounts that were given to you by the people who came from these various places, were there any major differences in their description of the, as you call it "cleansing" of their villages, or was it all much the same?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There were no major differences?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were hardly any differences. Maybe depending on the area, there could have been differences, the area in which the village in question was. Sometimes the army came down the local roads, and sometimes they came across meadows. But the point was always to round up a couple of houses, a hamlet, or a whole village, to start shooting at all sides at once, and then the army would subsequently enter the village, separate the men from the women, according to some logic that I couldn't understand, they separated the men and took part of the men to Trnopolje and part of them to Kozarac. They transported some of the men in vans. I did see a small bus once, and some walked. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain hiding in this general area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in the area for about a month. As far as I can remember, yes, about a month. While a number of people still remained there, a number of civilians, so when no operations were taking place, and then the cleansing operations, after a month, everyone was gone, and I was alone in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a number of documents that relate to the events of May and June of 1992 in the Kozarac area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we start by having a look, please, at an article that was publiced in Kozarski Vjesnik. It's been marked with the 65 ter number 192. I'm sorry, it's Glas, I'm sorry, dated the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could we please have the next number available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Court exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It would be Number S147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can take the map off the ELMO now. Thank you very much, usher. And perhaps, if we look at, on the ELMO, the English version while Mr. Sejmenovic keeps the Bosnian language version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an article that was published in Glas, apparently on the 30th of May, 1992, and the headline, there's a number of articles, but this one we can see though, was "Kozarac, the Serbian answer." Were you able to -- did you actually see any newspapers at the time, Mr. Sejmenovic, or not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no opportunity to read any newspapers at that time. Occasionally, I listened to the radio, but that was it. And only occasionally. I did not read newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the period in which I was hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I imagined that would be the case. This was an article reporting on a press conference given by the president of the SDS regional board, Radislav Vukic, and I think you've already told us you knew Mr. Vukic. I want to deal where he said in this press conference about Kozarac. He stated in about the third paragraph in the translation that "Bosnia will never again about a unitary state because it must be divided in three parts," called all Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina to join the front ranks of the Serbian army and the police. He went on to say this: "This is a defensive war and we must defend ourselves. We have always played with the black pieces, but this does not mean that in future, we will not apply the principle of reciprocity. All Muslims and Croats who provide illegal weapons should hand them in. We guarantee peace because we, the Krajina Serbs, are not extremists. We will not touch anybody, but we will answer every shot with a barrage." What this answer looks like has already been seen. Kozarac was liberated in three days..." Now first, Mr. Sejmenovic, from what you saw and your dealings with the SDS, do you agree with Mr. Vukic's assertion that this was a defensive war in which the Serbs were defending themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First of all, this witness clearly stated that he did not have any access to newspapers or any such documents. And subsequent, although we can assume that the witness obviously did not, at that time, have this particular article or document, so it would be far afield for this witness to give us factual observations that he may have experienced at the time or at any time shortly thereafter. Clearly this is an attempt to elicit an opinion testimony from this witness ten years later, applying what I believe are distorted facts that have not been properly read into the record and have not been read into the record completely by the OTP because there are sentences and words that precede where the OTP sought to stop, namely that the SDA party was being -- admitting certain factors. If the witness is going to be given documents this and asked to give an opinion, we ask that they provide us that in written form first under the proper notice requirements, governing the ICTY here. This witness was clear and unequivocal in his prior testimony and statement that he did not have access to any such newspapers which, in my opinion, respectfully, would include this one from the publication Glas dated the May 30th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, would you accept if the entire article of this newspaper is read out, and then the question then reads as follows: "Can you, on the basis of the facts and your own observations, state whether or not the observations made in this article are correct ones?"

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Formally, I never like to take a position that's contrary to the Court, so I'm hesitant somewhat. But quite frank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. And quite frankly, Your Honour, I think that with all due respect it would lead to a greater dangers and expose items that would necessitate an enormous length of time in cross because it's not just on one matter, but it's also showing a Nexus by Mr. Radislav Vukic which is the alleged person who made these comments with Dr. Stakic in this case. What does this have to do with what occurred from a man in Prijedor or from a man in Banja Luka, I should say, and what difference does it make if this individual witness had read it and gives us an opinion on it? And I say it respectfully with the witness being here. This witness is not an expert, is not competent to give expert testimony on this evidence. He can share with us if he believes, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 4715 to 4719. in his opinion, from what he observed at that time whether it was a defensive war or not. But to read the statement, and then to take the words provided in an article that appeared in Glas on the 30th of May, 1992, goes far afield to what this gentleman here is testifying to. Counsel could have asked him that question straight away and didn't, but choose instead to incorporate it as a formal opinion witness, and we object to that, and unfortunately I would like just the record to reflect that we would like to have either a standing objection on that, meaning for all questions, or if it's a matter of convenience for the Court, or I am going to have to formally object to each and every question that falls within what, I believe, is the scope of our prior oral motion soon to be a written motion, provided to the Court in connection with this very topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The objection is dismissed. And nevertheless, we would ask the OTP to concentrate on questions related to facts. But we have also to observe that the OTP, for example, referred specifically to the sentence: "Kozarac was liberated in three days." Apparently very close to that what the witness's testimony -- is testifying on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I just make a point. I know Your Honour wants to get on, but Mr. Ostojic does have a point on this. If he goes on getting up and objecting like this, we stop each time and have the argument. Your Honour, and each time, we have the same argument and each time I make the same response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I tell you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. During your absence, we decided that the Defence will file a motion substituting the former motion, and then we'll get a decision in principle on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know. I saw that. I read it when I came into court. But what I mean is for this moment, can we take it, as Mr. Ostojic says, he has got a standing objection to any questions that I ask relating to documents he says is out of this witness's expertise. Then we can get on quicker. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sejmenovic. Where were we? What was I asking you? Anybody? Let's get back to this article. Yes, Mr. Vukic, the head of the main board, SDS, in Banja Luka was saying that this was a defensive war. Now, from what you saw in Kozarac and other places, and indeed from your negotiations with the SDS, was that an accurate assertion?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an absolutely inaccurate assertion. I will like to say a couple of words more about this to help you understand the overall situation. Prior to the events in Prijedor, when the SDS arrested, arrested men of military age in Bosanski Novi and proclaimed Serbian -- the new Serbian government in Bosanski Novi, when the SDS took power in Prijedor in festive radio broadcasts and in announcement toss the citizens, they kept repeating that Prijedor was liberated as had happened in Bosanski Novi. I have mentioned Bosanski Novi because there were no war operations there. But the SDS proclaimed this liberation after they had rounded up the men, gave them yellow ribbons to wear, took them to the town stadium, and then expelled them or had them put in prison. So on that day, they announced the liberation of the town. Now I'm returning to the situation in Prijedor. Our main worry, and the aim of all our endeavours, was to in no way let anyone think that we were the enemies of the Serbian people. And we made great efforts to demonstrate this through our behaviour. When the operations began, when Kozarac was burned down, the first announcements on the radio were: "Victory has been won, Kozarac has been liberated." So this vocabulary was used wherever Serbs could succeed in their plans. So Vukic was not the first to say something like this. At least I had heard it from other people before in a number of places where Serbs were successful with their policies. What Vukic and these other people share is their common origin in the SDS. They were officials in the SDS. And he was not the first to say something like this. You could hear this sort of sentence many times before. Across the municipalities, on the Serb TV, broadcast from Banja Luka and on different shows and programmes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think you've answered the question I was going to ask you about the next part, "Kozarac was liberated in three days." And I'll read out for the purposes of Mr. Ostojic: "And in Sanski Most, the SDA president himself publicly apologized and said that his party was to blame for everything." Whilst were dealing with that, do you recall the leader of the SDA in Sanski Most apparently apologising and saying that his party was to blame for everything?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember anything like that. But I suppose he must have said something like that. I must have said it myself in the Omarska camp, when I was interviewed by Serb journalists and the Serbian television. It was a question of life and death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we just turn, please, in the translation, to one more sentence in this article, going back to Kozarac he said this: "A large number of extremists have been captured in the fighting at Kozarac, and other places in Krajina. But there are also a lot of women and children, who the Serbs are trying to take care of. If at all possible, we will try to exchange them for Serbs detained in Livno, Duvno, Derventa Modrica, and Travnik." And then, "the AR Krajina War Staff formed an agency for the exchange of prisoners, in which experts employed in the government of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina will work." What did you see the Serbs, who were operating in Kozarac, doing with the women and children?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sending the civilian population to Trnopolje. They said that there was a zone there, secured by the Serbian army, and that civilians, women, old people and men who were not extremists could go to Trnopolje and that nothing would happen to them there. I am talking about an announcement via the local radio. On the ground, things were different. People were compelled to do things there, killed, and threatened and expelled in the direction of Trnopolje. Later on, convoys of civilians from other parts of Prijedor started arriving in Trnopolje. And then a month or a month and a half later, the population was transferred from Trnopolje, supposedly to the free area of Gracanica, the BH army-controlled territory. And then via Banja Luka towards Travnik -- via Banja Luka and Vlasic towards Travnik. The Serb authorities did this either by train and by freight train which would reach Trnopolje and would be filled by civilians there. And later on, they started doing this, using trucks and buses. I watched some of these operations myself. Both while I was outside the camp and while I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll come on back to the transport in a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, I should say, is that document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do object as to both foundation and to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We regard it necessary to have the entire article admitted into evidence, also, first of all, to give the Defence a chance during cross-examination to come back to other parts of this entire document. Therefore, the English translation is admitted into evidence as S147A, and from the B/C/S, we have the document ending with the number 942. Only the upper part, the four left-hand columns, including this article on Kozarac, admitted to this. And I ask the OTP, is it necessary to have 943 admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that was only to show the date of the article, because otherwise it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can read this on 942. And therefore admitted into evidence as S147B only the article in the first four columns including both boxed texts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, whilst -- before you went to Trnopolje, did you hear about any kind of attack on Prijedor town itself?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. And I also saw the smoke coming from the direction of Prijedor. I heard some unofficial information on the attack on Prijedor, the information which I heard from the people who were fleeing and who were able to reach Prijedor from Kozarac, or the people who happened to be in the area of Sivci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I'd like you, please, to look at another article, this time from Kozarski Vjesnik. It is marked with the 64 ter number -- 65 ter number I should say, 223. And it's an article dated the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and read out the entire document, in order not to confuse.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to, Your Honour, on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The article is dated the 5th of June, 1992 and is headed: "Removing the Consequences of Attack." And it states -- I'm sorry: "Subject: Attack on Prijedor." I don't know if that appears in the B/C/S. "At its meeting on Sunday evening, the Crisis Staff discussed the current course of the operation aimed at disarming the Muslim paramilitaries, and a number of problems related to it. Over the last few days, the Crisis Staff has undertaken a number of measures to remove the consequences of military operations, from clearing up the battlefield to looking after the people who left their homes. The large-scale operation proceeded successfully and continued yesterday in the local communes in the towns -- in the town and outlying areas. In the town itself, the consequences of attacks by the Muslim fundamentalists were being removed. After their attack on the town, the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina undertook the necessary measures to neutralise the effects of their operations and defend the vital facilities, the town, and its population. In street fighting, 16 defenders were killed and 16 were wounded. The largest number of soldiers in the army of the Serbian Republic of BH were killed by fire of an ambush laid overnight by the paramilitaries. Others, perfidiously from the back and still others, treacherously from the windows of apartment buildings. The losses on the side of the attackers were far greater. Infiltrated groups have been completely destroyed while individual snipers were still active on the streets of Prijedor yesterday. The army launched an operation yesterday to remove and neutralise the snipers, in which two soldiers were wounded. At its meeting, the Crisis Staff also discussed problems of temporarily displaced persons taking shelter in camps because of the war operations. The Crisis Staff concluded that the operation to collect illegal weapons should also continue in the town area. At present, all the necessary steps are being taken to restore normal life to the town and outlying areas." Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, having read that article, what was the situation that you understood was taking place from what you saw and from the persons that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Kozarac, parts of the Territorial Defence, which I spoke about, in Kozarac were elsewhere in the territory of Prijedor, such as Ljubija, Hambarine, Rizvanovici, and Biscani. It is true that they had fewer members, because it's not such a large area. But they were organised officially as Territorial Defence there. After the attack on Kozarac, all communication with those elements of the Territorial Defence was severed. As it was stated in the article, Kozarac was destroyed within three days, together with its population. Those elements of the Territorial Defence in the other region of Prijedor inhabited by non-Serb population were to a certain extent organised. When we heard about the attack on Prijedor, and I said that we had heard about it while we were there with the refugee column, we assumed that the Territorial Defence from Hambarine, Rizvanovici, Brdo, or Ljubija, had undertaken some kind of action, some kind of operation in Prijedor. Once again, we heard various kinds of ultimatum over the radio, and we heard, as it is stated in the article, that a certain number of soldiers had been killed, but we did not hear about any civilian casualties. This was not typically broadcast over the radio. Only soldiers who had been killed in these street fights were mentioned. The resistance was crushed in one day, and that was the end of the resistance in the area of Prijedor, generally speaking. As for the details regarding the manner in which it was carried out and the number of people who took part, I don't know anything about that because we were, practically speaking, completely isolated and found ourselves in a totally different area of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said that the resistance was crushed in one day. Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that on the Serb radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for the admission of that document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objections, Your Honour, and also that the testimony relied solely on hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The English version is admitted into evidence as S148. But we have to take care, opposed to that what was read out, on page 37, line 8, it reads: "And still others by gunfire from the windows of apartment buildings." As regards the B/C/S version, it's only admitted into evidence, the upper part, including the article, starting from the left-hand side, the first four columns, and there is no need to admit into evidence the second copy of the same document with the -- ending with the number 260. So it remains 148B, the document ending with the registration number 365. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In connection with the same event, could you look, please, now at the next document marked with the 65 ter number 225.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We don't have 225, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The same is true for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And us as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I'll ignore it. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It has already been admitted, Your Honour. It's S70. Your Honour, if it has already been admitted, I'm not going to bother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S70 has already been read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I won't trouble. I'm trying to deal with documents that haven't been dealt with before. However, 226, can I ask, Rule 65 ter 226, also admitted, is it? Yes, also been dealt with, I gather. All right. No, but I think -- I gather -- yes, all right. It may have been read, but I'd still like to ask the witness about it, please. It's S71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be aware that it was read out already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate that. I gather it has just been read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I want to ask you about this document, Mr. Sejmenovic, is this: It states that the Crisis Staff discussed at its meeting of the 6th of June, 1992, the security situation in Pecani and other parts of the town, and then they issued a conclusion, relating to security at the Prijedor hospital. That part of town, can I just ask you this: What sort of area was it? Was it ethnically mixed, or was it Muslim only?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority was Serb, as far as Pecani. As for the area in which the main hospital in Prijedor was situated, the population was almost a hundred per cent Serb as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, now you spoke earlier about what was happening to women and children and the like after these operations in the various areas. Could you look, now, please at document with the 65 ter number 239, which I don't think has been admitted yet. No. Now, this is a document which apparently has been sent to the local police, because if one looks at it, it's signed by Zupljanin, and at the bottom, one can see -- I'm sorry, I should start at the top. Attention, all persons concerned, chief. And then after the signature--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you continue, could you please help us understand the document. We have English document of one page before us, and then we have in B/C/S four pages before us. What are we referring to? Is this a fax?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it is a -- I'm not actually sure. It looks, though, it may well be a telex-type thing. We would have to get the original out of the evidence vault, and Your Honour would probably like us to do that. But we've translated, it looks like, just the first two pages of whatever this telefax. In other words, 00478710 to 711. There are two pages of the English, Your Honour should have. The second page simply says: "Chief of centre, Stojan Zupljanin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it necessary for the OTP to work with such doubtful documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why is it doubtful, Your Honour, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because we can't identify what is really the original, where we have translation of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It appears to me that the -- it's a translation of -- we can get the original document out. Your Honour, I'm just inquiring as to, it comes from -- all right. Your Honour, we're just checking where it comes from. We have a feeling it's from the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to proceed without this document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just lost my...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Sejmenovic, leaving documents for the moment -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, I will come back to that document. We'll get the original from the evidence vault. It comes from the Prijedor Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, moving along, Mr. Sejmenovic, we'll come back to that on another occasion, how long did you actually hide out for?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take into account the period which I spent in the house of this woman who was hiding me, and the period of time which I spent alone, up until my arrival in the camp, the total would amount to two months approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did ask you that before, but I had forgot that. Now, eventually, did you go to -- back to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After all of the villages had been cleansed of their residents, I spent some time alone in the area that I mentioned, in the vicinity of these houses. Actually, in the vicinity of a Serbian checkpoint. I slept in some very thick shrubbery some 50 metres away from the Serb guards because I thought that was the safest place for me to hide since they were searching the surrounding houses and the area generally. Having spent some 15 days over there, I set out in the direction of Trnopolje. And it took me about 15 days to reach Trnopolje, that is, the area close to the place where I used to live, close to the place where we have some property, my family. And it was from that vantage point that I observed the Trnopolje camp for a while, its guards, the personnel, the access roads and so on and so forth. And after that, I actually went to the camp. I came close to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any barrier of any kind around the camp as you were observing it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was perfectly familiar with the area in question, because it is situated in the vicinity of my house. The entrance to the camp, from the western side, from the direction of Prijedor, was 10 metres away from my house. And it stretched up to the Trnopolje/Kozarac Road. This is where I used to live, and I knew the area very well. As for the barriers that existed at the time, and these barriers had been there even before the war, one side of the complex had a wire fence. One side had some metal fence interspersed with wire fence, but the third side did not have any fence or wire. It was completely open, but the borderline, the boundary, was the Trnopolje/Prijedor Road itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any guards round the camp at all?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. When I approached the camp, I saw them posted on several spots. I also saw some machine-gun nests, the checkpoints. When I entered the camp, I inquired further about this, and I learned that there were such places even elsewhere around the camp, the area which I was not able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The guards that you saw, police or military or both?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military. From time to time, I saw policemen coming to the camp. On one occasion, I remember seeing them going to the camp, taking a group of people from there. I could see that because I was very close. It was a mixed group of personnel, both police and military. As for the checkpoints and machine-gun nests, they were manned exclusively by soldiers. I'm talking only about those I was able to observe with my own eyes. There were other places in respect of which I heard that there were machine-gun nests and checkpoints, but this is not something that I saw personally. The people who saw this told me that they were manned by the military. The military was also at the checkpoint near Petrov Gaj. They were always referring to soldiers. Nobody made any mention of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you decide to go into the camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous testimonies, in the Tadic case, for example, I spoke in detail about this. Since I was familiar with the terrain, I knew how to come close to the camp and to see what was going on without anyone else noticing me. And I realised that the situation was not -- that the situation was chaotic, that the men were not kept separated from women. And I saw a spot where I was able to come really close to the fence on the eastern side of the camp, so I made this decision. I went up to the fence. The spot looked pretty safe to me. It was overgrown with some shrubbery, and I knew I could hide there for a while, even sleep. So I spent some time observing the situation inside the camp. And as I said, it did look chaotic to me. I recognised some people, and I decided to go in. My first question was whether it was possible for me to hide there, or whether it would be better for me flee. And a neighbour of mine told me that the whole camp was supposed to be evacuated to the village of Gracanica. He said that there were very many people inside and all I had to do was cover myself with something and try to avoid recognition. But he also said, as far as I was concerned, they were trying to find me in the camp. They searched for me in the camp a month ago, and he said that they thought I was dead. So I decided to sneak in and to try and leave the area in one of the convoys departing from there. But it turned out that I was wrong, that this was not possible, and after several days, I left the camp the same way I got in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The days that you were in the camp, what were the conditions like there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very bad. Food was not organised. There was an oven there, but hardly enough for one tenth of the people who were there. The people who were in the camp, or the doctors who were in the camp, tried to organise some sort of medical assistance. They succeeded in obtaining an approval from the command of the camp for some people to be issued with a permit to go to their own homes and bring back flour so they could cook in the camp. It was in this way that we had supplies of flour, but those were insufficient in terms of quantity. The approvals to join convoys on their way out were being bought and sold. When I entered the camp, they asked for 300 German mark per person. The price had previously been about 2.000 German mark. I was advised by some of my friends to give them 300 German mark, to dress up as a woman, disguise myself as a woman so that I could be allowed to join one of those convoys. I only had a hundred German mark on me, so this was not a possibility that I was in a position to consider.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you decided to leave the camp. Did you go back to where you had been hiding?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason for me to leave the camp very soon was that the group of people who were staying with me in that part of the camp were taken away, and as we thought, shot. It later turned out that all six of them, those people were relatives among themselves, three times two brothers by the name of Foric indeed had been shot. I slept near them for three days just before that, and I talked to them. At first, I thought that the Serbs had realised that I was there, and that that may have been the reason why they had taken those people away. And now they were waiting to see who else would contact me in order to kill that person. One of the people from that group, I asked him whether he thought this was the case, and he said he didn't think so. So after this, I made up my mind to leave the camp in the middle of the night, and I did it around half past 2.00. And again, I reached the place from which I had observed the camp several days before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, did you go -- I'm sorry. Did you go back then, to the camp again after a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an agreement with my friend from Kamicani. He had also made up his mind to leave the camp and to head for Kozara or for Grmec. However, he was scared to leave because he was afraid that the whole camp would later be evacuated, so he was afraid of missing his chance to live, to reach the free territory without any risk. The camp commanders, the Prijedor radio station, as well as the Serbian Red Cross, who would all occasionally come to the camp were speaking about this possibility. Our agreement was that he would take me to -- that he would reach me at a place around a 100, 150 metres from the camp with a message as to whether there was a mass evacuation planned. Or just leave the camp the same way I left it and bring me food to last me several days. So the same day we agreed that he should send the message or food, I set out for that place. I did reach the place, but I could neither find a message nor the food that he had promised. That for me was an obvious sign that an evacuation was being planned, because there were a dozen empty buses in the camp by that time. I thought that perhaps he was not willing to take this risk, and I thought this was the day of the mass evacuation which was the reason why I got back into the camp the same way I used to before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once you got back into the camp, did you discover that your presence in the camp had been noticed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Immediately upon re-entering the camp, I contacted my neighbour and friend, Adim Trnjanin. When he saw me, he began to cry. He kept saying: "It's over, it's over. Mevludin, our time is out. The 15 of us, we had been shut up. Some of us had been beaten. They gave us 48 hours to tell them where you were. They said that if we didn't say, they would kill us all. They sent out two intervention platoons to search the area between the Roslja [phoen] field and on to Gornji Sivci and Krajinska Crka [phoen]," because someone had told them that I was in that area. So I went back to the camp in the morning, and their deadline was to expire at I think 10.00 or 11.00. I told him to just give me half an hour to take leave of a number of people and to leave a message for my relatives who might survive. I told him to go get Captain or Colonel Slavko, who was the chief of the guard duty around the camp. I sat down on a stone alone as I was. He went and came back with this Slavko. Slavko then approached me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did this Slavko, in fact, take you -- was he on his own or was somebody else with him?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came alone. Adim went to the camp command building. He came out with Slavko, and then turned to the right where the remaining camp inmates were and Slavko headed for a clearing where I was sitting. He approached me, and he took me towards the camp command building, outside which Major Slobodan Kuruzovic, wearing a uniform, was already standing. He was the then camp commander. It was the same Kuruzovic that I had already referred to in reply to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I was just going to ask you. This was somebody you knew?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Mr. Kuruzovic whom I had last seen at a meeting with the SDS in Prijedor when they gave us the ultimatum that I had told you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now you were taken in to see Major, whatever he was, Kuruzovic. Were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly. In Trnopolje itself, I was only questioned briefly. First they began beating me, but then Kuruzovic said: "It's enough. We will receive our information later." There was a soldier who ran in my direction, and he asked: "Major, shall we beat him right now?" And the Major told him in as many words: "Sod off, we'll get our information later." And he went to the house of one of my neighbours which had been transformed to serve as the camp command building. He took me there and started asking me questions. He and two or three other officers, but this only lasted very briefly, maybe for about ten minutes. I only know that he and another person that he spoke to on the phone, and Slavko, whom I've also mentioned, could not agree whether they would take me to a military prison or to a prison for civilians. So this gave rise to a discussion that lasted for a while. I don't know what the result was, but I know that after a while, with some materials they had found in my house, a box full of materials, they put me in a car and took me to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when they took to you Prijedor, did they use the main road or the secondary road?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used the secondary road, the Trnopolje/Prijedor -- that is Omarska/Trnopolje/Prijedor Road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. On your drive to Prijedor, what did you notice, if anything, about the houses?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leaving the camp itself, and then on to the village of Petkovici, the houses had marks of fire shots on their walls, and some of the houses were burned. A couple of houses were burned. And most were just covered by artillery shots with all the glass smashed. Going towards Prijedor from Trnopolje down this old secondary road, there wasn't a lot of Serbian population in that area. When you enter the village of Petkovici, there Serb territory begins except for a small area further down after Petkovici. And there, in that area, there were no signs of destruction. And the same all the way to Prijedor, that is Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you were in Prijedor, did you go anywhere near Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stopped just opposite Keraterm in a place where the old road that we're talking about, very near Keraterm, meets the main road, the Banja Luka/Prijedor main road. We went into some sort of a yard in the industrial zone opposite Keraterm. There was the headquarters of one of the main Prijedor enterprises. I'm not sure which one it was. But then at that time it was used by the military police. And opposite that building was the Keraterm camp. They stopped outside the police building. There was a soldier sitting next to me. And we waited for about ten minutes in the car while Slavko and Brane Beric, who sat in front with Slavko, went inside the building. During this time, I could observe the Keraterm camp, or at least the part that you could see from the car which was most of it. I saw the camp inmates across the road. This may have lasted for about ten minutes at the most before they returned. I started talking to the soldier who was sitting next to me, and we exchanged a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just have a look at the map, please, for a moment, with some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unmarked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't the faintest idea what the exhibit number is. Your Honour, I'm sure that Your Honours' registry must have the photograph without the legend below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, we don't have. We didn't admit into evidence a similar document with indicating --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. It has already been done. Your Honour, there is now one prepared which has nothing to describe the photographs, so I would ask that that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it could be first shown to the Defence, please, and then to the Bench. I take it that both the Defence and the Bench will receive copies of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't catch what Your Honour said, so I was waiting for it to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you see -- looking at those photographs, could you identify which photograph -- whether you can see a photograph of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does it have a number?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can identify its position on the map. Can I just have a minute to check. I think it's photograph number 7. Just a minute, please. I think it's photograph number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wonder what you want me to do with this. He has got it correctly, and we removed any indications from the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's on the transcript. We can find on the transcript that the witness identified, pointed to number 7. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, where you were taken to Mr. Sejmenovic, you've described to us. Is the area anywhere that we can see in the photograph there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pointing at it. This area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you go back --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the pointer is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- number 7. In that photograph, can we see the area to which you were taken, where you were able to see the inmates of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Off the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right, off the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This document should have number S150?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 149. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour, with respect to the photograph number 7. But then I don't know what the other photographs relate to, so we'll reserve our right to object at that time, if it comes up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you've got a map which tells you what all the photographs are, a separate one. It's the same as the one you had originally, but we've just taken out from it the legend. It tells you what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see the objections. We have the photos also available in another and better format. But nevertheless, it is tendered by the OTP and admitted into evidence as S149.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honour, that the description was S2 [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Sejmenovic, you saw some of the inmates. How were you able to see them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw many people by the fence, many rows of people. The place was, in a manner of speaking, teeming with people along the fence and also deep into this area comprising the factory. I saw many people, most of them were naked from the waist up. They were skinny, emaciated. I looked several times, and I tried not to show that I was looking because of the soldier who were sitting to my right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these approximately ten minutes, Slavko and Brane Beric came back. They got into the car, and we drove off to Prijedor centre where the police station was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, at the police station, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station, I was first taken to a room. I was asked a number of questions by a man I had known before the war. Sometimes we had coffee together. Then a soldier walked in who started to beat me. He also kicked me. He hit me with a club. And then after I fell to the ground, he pulled the belt from my trousers, tied it up around my neck, and poked fun at me saying that I was a deputy to the assembly and I needed a tie to wear. And then he dragged me by the belt to another office where an older policeman and an older man wearing civilian clothes were. I knew them both by sight, and then these two continued to question me, which took a bit longer. I may have stayed about one and a half hours inside that office, after which I was taken back to my prison cell. I was beaten again outside the cell, but they no longer went into the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was anything said to you before the beating started or took place?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean outside the cell?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean -- sorry. Just sticking for a moment to the beating in the office, the room. Did anybody say anything to you before the soldiers walked in and started to beat you as to why they were beating --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This colleague of mine, the man I told you about, the one I knew, he poked fun at me because I was a deputy. I was dirty and my shoes were torn. I had no shoelaces. "Why don't I wash up," he told me. "Where is my suit?" "Where is my tie?" He abused like that for several minutes, and then Dragomir Saponja came in and did the job he was probably sent over there to do. After I had been beaten there, they started questioning me in the other office. And the first sentence spoken by the inspector was - let me make this clear; I'm almost quoting him - he said: "You're a fundamentalist. You can claim you're not, but you are, and your father was one, too, which means that you are one." And then they began. Where was I born? When was I born? So the basic personal information. And then charges of fundamentalism, fundamentalist policy, and this went on for a while. They took a break, and after the break they questioned me again for a while. Minutes were -- a record was drawn up during the questioning. I behaved as best I could, trying with my answers to save my own life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had anything like this ever happened to you before, an unprovoked beating like this and this sort of interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did receive a blow or two in Trnopolje itself. When I surrendered and when Slavko took me to Kuruzovic, I did receive seven or eight blows there. But at that point Kuruzovic told the other man: "Sod off, we'll get our information later." The same happened to me in Omarska when I was taken there. First, I was taken to the white house as the camp inmates called it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to deal with this part, because I think that will do for today. You say you received some slaps in Trnopolje. This, you say, was a much greater beating. Was that the first time you had received anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was in Trnopolje. I was hit several times. And then the beating I took in Prijedor was much worse. I fell down to the ground while I was being beaten. And then while I was going questioned outside the prison cell, they really beat me black and blue. I could even stand up for a while afterwards. And then they threw my body into the cell. After about ten days, I partly recovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shall call it a day. And the trial stands adjourned until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's on. Until tomorrow, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of June, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
